narration: The model reports a suspicious R² of exactly 1.0 on a 1000-row sample (ample for reliable estimation). Two columns carry near-perfect correlations with the target: log_target_v2 (Spearman 0.99899) and near_target_proxy (Pearson 0.99874), both far beyond every other feature, which merely cluster between -0.04 and +0.03. Although the exact-prediction match rate is 0.0, a near-unit R² together with features that essentially encode the target strongly indicates target leakage rather than a legitimately learned relationship. Recommend dropping these columns from the modeling set and re-evaluating honest performance.

The reported r2 of 1.0 is almost certainly leakage. Two columns in the evidence set are near-perfect copies of the target: log_target_v2 correlates 0.998993270993271 (Spearman) and near_target_proxy correlates 0.998736261844771 (Pearson) with the target, while every other feature is essentially uncorrelated (|r| <= 0.041 across feature_12, feature_10, feature_5, feature_9, feature_8, feature_4, feature_7, feature_6). With 1000 rows the sample is large enough that these values are not sampling noise, and the deterministic tool already flagged these two as candidate leak columns. An R2 of exactly 1.0 with no perfect string match (perfect_match_rate 0.0) points to a continuous near-copy of the target driving the fit rather than an untrained/duplicate row artifact. Recommend dropping log_target_v2 and near_target_proxy and re-fitting; also verify lineage/metadata to confirm they were derived from the label and check for target encoding computed before the train/test split.

The model reports a perfect r2 of 1.0 on a 1000-row sample, which is implausible for genuine predictive signal. Two candidate columns, log_target_v2 (spearman 0.99899) and near_target_proxy (pearson 0.99874), are almost perfectly correlated with the target, while all remaining features sit near zero correlation (|r| <= 0.040). This pattern strongly indicates target leakage: the model's apparent perfect score is driven by columns that encode the target rather than by legitimate predictors. The perfect_match_rate is 0.0, so the leak is via near-copies/correlated encodings rather than exact row duplication, but the correlations are so close to 1 that leakage is the only plausible explanation. Recommended: drop or audit log_target_v2 and near_target_proxy, verify their provenance (e.g., whether they were derived from the target after the fact or computed with future information), and re-evaluate the metric without them.

The reported r2 of exactly 1.0 is the red flag. Two candidate columns stand out: log_target_v2 correlates 0.99899 (spearman) with the target, and near_target_proxy correlates 0.99874 (pearson). By contrast, every other feature has essentially no linear relationship with the target, with absolute correlations under 0.041 (feature_12 -0.04045, feature_10 -0.03543, feature_5 -0.03470, feature_9 0.03038, feature_8 -0.02793, feature_4 -0.02151, feature_7 -0.01969, feature_6 0.01337). This bimodal pattern — two columns near 1.0 and everything else near 0 — is the classic signature of target leakage rather than genuine signal. The perfect_match_rate of 0.0 does not rule out leakage; it only means no exact string-level match, and log_target_v2 being a monotone (log) transform of the target would not match exactly yet would still be nearly perfectly predictive. Notably, the model's r2 = 1.0 exceeds what even a 0.99899 correlation would produce on its own, further suggesting these columns encode the label itself. Verdict: leakage likely, driven by log_target_v2 and near_target_proxy.
